title: Collaborative Document Editor
prompt:
Design a Google Docs-style editor where multiple people edit the same rich-text document simultaneously.

Functional requirements:
- Real-time co-editing; everyone converges to the same document state.
- Show collaborators' cursors and selections.
- Offline edits merge when the user reconnects.
- Full version history with the ability to restore; comments anchored to text.

Scale:
- 50M daily active users, 5M documents open concurrently.
- Most documents have 1-3 editors; some have up to 100 simultaneous editors and thousands of viewers.
- Edit operations: about 1 per second per active typist.

Questions to answer:
1. Operational transformation or CRDTs: how does each guarantee convergence, and which would you choose?
2. How do clients and servers exchange operations, and where is the authoritative order decided?
3. How are documents and history persisted efficiently?
4. How do you scale to millions of open documents and handle a very popular document?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Assume 10M active typists x 1 op/s = 10M ops/s peak globally, batched by clients every ~100-200 ms into far fewer messages.
- Op log: ~50 bytes per op, 10M/s would be ~40 TB/day raw; compaction via snapshots is essential.

OT VS CRDT
- OT: clients send ops based on a known revision; the server transforms incoming ops against ops committed since that revision and assigns a total order. Simple data, needs a central sequencer per document. Proven (Google Docs).
- CRDT (RGA, Yjs, Automerge): each character/element has a unique ID; merges are commutative so any order converges. Works peer-to-peer and offline; costs metadata overhead (tombstones, IDs) and memory.
- Reasonable choice: server-centered OT, or a CRDT with a server relay for ordering and persistence. CRDT is stronger for offline-first.

PROTOCOL (OT, central sequencer)
- Client applies ops locally immediately (optimistic), keeps at most one outstanding batch, and sends {doc_id, base_revision, ops}.
- Document session server transforms against newer ops, assigns revision N+1, appends to the log, ACKs the sender, and broadcasts to other clients, who transform against their pending local ops.
- Cursors/presence are ephemeral messages, not persisted, throttled.

ROUTING
- Each open document is owned by exactly one session server (consistent hashing on doc_id with a lease in a coordination service). All editors connect, via WebSocket gateways, to that owner. Single owner makes ordering trivial and avoids cross-node coordination.
- On owner failure, a new owner takes the lease, loads the latest snapshot plus log tail, and clients resync from their last ACKed revision.

STORAGE
- Append-only op log per document (wide-column store keyed by doc_id, revision) plus periodic snapshots (every N ops) in object storage.
- Load = latest snapshot + replay ops after it. Version history = named snapshots plus the log.
- Comments anchored to stable positions (CRDT IDs or OT-transformed anchors).

POPULAR DOCUMENTS
- Separate editors from viewers: viewers subscribe via a fan-out tier (pub/sub) that relays committed ops, so the owner only handles editors.
- Batch broadcasts; cap simultaneous editors per document with graceful degradation to view mode.

PITFALLS
- Last-writer-wins on the whole document; loses edits.
- Using wall-clock timestamps to order concurrent ops.
- Unbounded op logs or CRDT tombstones without compaction.
- Permission changes must take effect on live sessions (revoke the connection).
